newsitem.title: USA: US, EU meat deal possible, but not seen for poultry.
newsitem.headline: US, EU meat deal possible, but not seen for poultry.

text.p: An agreement between the United States and European Union on meat import regulations may be reached soon, but it is not likely to include any settlement of poultry issues, industry sources said Tuesday.
"We're not optimistic. We have not been able to agree on some areas that we thought we could," said Julie De Young of the National Turkey Federation.

De Young and other poultry industry sources said that decontamination issues, and the use of chlorine by the U.S. industry, have not been worked out, and they said they anticipated Washington and Brussels to avoid escalating the trade war by working out a deal on everything but poultry.

Washington has threatened to remove over 100 European meat and poultry packing plants from its list of approved exporters on April 30 if a deal has not been reached. The action would halt some $300 million worth of European meat shipments -- mostly pork products from Denmark -- to the United States.

On April 1, EU imposed new rules which have halted all U.S. poultry shipments to Europe -- worth some $50 million annually -- and those regulations would likely stay in place if negotiators agreed to a deal that did not include poultry.
Europe has threatened swift retaliation if Washington delists the European plants on April 30.

U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said earlier Tuesday he would call EU Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler to discuss the situation. Glickman said, "We are within striking distance" of a pact.

At issue in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks was whether the two sides, which use different meat inspection regimes, could agree on a method for determining that each other's products were safe.

Besides the poultry issues, the EU has asked for retroactive "regionalization" on the U.S. part. Glickman said retroactive regionalization could be achieved only by the lengthy U.S. rulemaking process.
U.S. meat industry officials said most issues pertaining to red meat have been resolved, and they were pushing for an agreement without poultry.
"We hope poultry can get their problems resolved, but we have to do what's best for beef and pork ... We can't be held hostage to any other product," said a meat industry official.
